title: GDGoC Admin
summary: An open-source platform that designs, issues, emails and verifies event certificates for 20+ GDG on Campus chapters across Egypt.

sections.title: The use case
sections.body:
Google Developer Groups on Campus chapters run workshops, study jams and hackathons all year, and every event ends the same way: each attendee is owed a certificate.

GDGoC Admin is where chapter leaders do that work. A leader designs the certificate once, drops in the attendee sheet, and the platform renders a personalised certificate for every row, emails it from the chapter's own address, and gives each one a public page anyone can use to check it is genuine. A super admin oversees every chapter, and good templates can be shared so a new chapter starts from a design that already works.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
At GDG on Campus NCTU, every event meant hours of copy-pasting names into a design file, exporting one certificate at a time, and sending emails by hand. The work grew in a straight line with attendance, so the bigger the community got, the worse it became.

It was also fragile. A typo meant redoing a certificate, designs drifted between organisers, and once a certificate left the inbox there was no way to prove it was real. Every chapter across Egypt was solving the same problem on its own.

sections.title: Features
sections.body:
- **Visual certificate editor**: drag, resize, rotate and layer text, images, vector shapes and QR codes on a canvas, Canva-style. Text layers can be *dynamic*, bound to a variable such as the recipient's name.
- **Bulk issuance**: import recipients from CSV or Excel, optionally compute cells with spreadsheet-style formulas, and issue the whole batch in one run.
- **Direct mail to recipients**: branded HTML emails written in a rich-text editor, with variable placeholders, sent through each chapter's own SMTP (manual, Google or Microsoft OAuth) with the certificate attached.
- **Public verification**: every certificate carries a QR code that opens a public page confirming it, with a proper link preview when shared.
- **Dynamic images**: personalised social cards and banners rendered on the fly from a single URL with query parameters, with no batch needed.
- **Versioned, shareable templates**: every save is an immutable version, and templates and email designs can be published for other chapters to clone.
- **PDF and PNG output**, including a print-safe colour mode.
- **Font library**: upload custom fonts, with automatic fallback to Google Fonts.
- **Roles and audit log**: super admins and chapter leaders, whitelist-only sign-up, and a record of who did what.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body:
A monorepo with a **Go + Fiber** API and a **React 19 + React Router v7** single-page app, on **PostgreSQL** and **Redis**, shipped as Docker images to **AWS ECS** via **ECR**.

- **Domain-driven API.** Each area (templates, issuance, mail, verification, dynamic images, chapters, users) is its own package with the same handler → service → repository layering.
- **Designs as data.** The editor, built on Konva, saves a certificate as a JSON scene. Each save is an immutable version, and a batch snapshots the version it was issued under, so an old certificate always renders exactly as it was issued.
- **A pure-Go renderer.** Certificates are drawn server-side with `tdewolff/canvas`, handling text, images, gradients, bezier shapes and QR codes with no C dependencies, which keeps the container a small static binary. The same renderer powers certificates and dynamic images.
- **Batches off the request path.** Issuing a batch hands its ID to an in-process queue that a pool of goroutines drains, sending each email concurrently. Rendering is lazy: a certificate is rasterised the first time it is fetched, then cached, so a big batch never stalls on image work nobody has asked for yet.
- **Layered variables.** Emails and certificates resolve placeholders in a fixed order: recipient values, then batch-level overrides, then system values such as the certificate ID and verification link.
- **Auth by Kayan**, a headless identity platform I built, providing OIDC, multi-provider OAuth and role-based access control.

Frontend: Konva, Tiptap, TanStack Query, React Hook Form + Zod, Radix UI, Tailwind CSS. Backend: Fiber, GORM, go-redis, tdewolff/canvas, go-qrcode, gofpdf.

sections.title: Results
sections.body:
The platform is live in production, used by **20+ GDG on Campus chapters across Egypt**, and has issued **more than 1,000 certificates** so far.

What used to be hours of manual work per event is now one design, one spreadsheet and one click, and every certificate can be verified by anyone who receives it. It is open source, so any chapter organiser can run it or build on it.

title: IoT Telemetry Platform
summary: End-to-end pipeline carrying sensor readings from ESP32 nodes to a live dashboard.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Readings were collected by hand from devices in the field, so problems were only discovered days after they happened.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: Firmware batches readings and publishes over MQTT with a store-and-forward buffer for dropouts. An ingest service normalises and writes to a time-series store; the dashboard subscribes to a websocket channel fed by the same pipeline.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: Operators see device state within seconds, and the buffer means a lost uplink no longer means lost data.

title: Offline-First Mobile App
summary: Flutter application that stays usable with no connection and reconciles on reconnect.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Field staff worked in places with no reliable signal, and the existing app was unusable the moment it lost the network.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: Local SQLite is the source of truth. Writes queue as intents and replay on reconnect, with last-write-wins per field and an explicit conflict view for the cases that rule cannot settle.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: The application works identically offline, and sync conflicts became visible and resolvable instead of silent.

title: Data Extraction Pipeline
summary: Scraping and normalisation system for sources that actively resist automation.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: The data needed for a client's pricing decisions lived across sites with no APIs, inconsistent markup, and aggressive rate limits.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: Per-source adapters isolate the parts that break, feeding a shared normalisation layer. A scheduler paces requests per host, and a schema check quarantines suspect rows rather than letting them through.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: A source changing its markup now breaks one adapter instead of the pipeline, and bad data is caught before it reaches the client.

title: Desktop Inventory Tool
summary: Cross-platform desktop client for stock control on machines with no internet access.

sections.title: Problem
sections.body: Stock was tracked in a spreadsheet that two people edited on different machines, so the counts disagreed by the end of most weeks.

sections.title: Approach
sections.body: A single-binary desktop application over an embedded database, with every mutation written as an append-only entry so a disputed count can be traced back rather than argued about.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: One source of truth, and a history that explains how each number got there.
